utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Technically, your solemn declaration that you made when you appeared for the first time is still valid. But for reminder, I would like you to take the solemn declaration again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: Good morning, President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's just make short pauses between my sentences and yours. Did you provide my Defence team an additional statement, a supplemental statement, that is?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up 1D49025. It shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the supplemental statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it accurately reflect what you said to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions today here in the courtroom, would your answers in essence be the same?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes, they would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I would like to tender this statement under seal, and the redacted version of the statement is 1D49050.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit both versions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D49025 receives Exhibit Number D4191, under seal. 65 ter number 1D49050 receives Exhibit Number D4192.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I'm going to read a short summary of the supplemental statement provided by Mr. Sveto Veselinovic in English. [In English] Sveto Veselinovic is testifying at my trial today for the second time. After the re-instatement of the genocide charge contained in Count 1 of the indictment, Mr. Veselinovic has been asked to comment on the evidence of Prosecution Witness KDZ051, who claimed that in around September 1992, in Rogatica, he asked Mr. Veselinovic what would happen to the Muslims. According to the Witness KDZ051, Mr. Veselinovic responded that the Muslims were going to disappear from the territory and that Mr. Veselinovic had meetings with Radovan Karadzic in Pale and that it had been decided that one-third of Muslims would be killed, one-third would be converted to the Orthodox religion, and a third would leave on their own. Mr. Veselinovic states that he does not know Witness KDZ051 and that he never had such a conversation with Witness KDZ051 or anyone else. He further states that he had never had a conversation with Dr. Karadzic in which it was stated that one-third of Muslims would be killed, one-third would be converted to the Orthodox religion, and a third would leave on their own. Mr. Veselinovic states that he did not see or speak to Dr. Karadzic between January 1992 and the autumn 1993, and that those sentiments do not represent what he understood to be Dr. Karadzic's views in any way, shape, or form. Mr. Veselinovic states that he never had any indication, directly or indirectly, that Dr. Karadzic favoured the destruction of the Bosnian Muslims in whole or in part. [Interpretation] This is a short summary and at this moment I have no further questions for Mr. Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson, I take it you requested 45 minutes for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, when you testified back in February, I asked you about an article you authored in the "Politika" publication, where you stated: "We have a message for all those who are preparing dirty war plans that the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina are ready and that 1941 will never be repeated." And you confirmed in your examination that your reference to 1941 was a reference to the destruction of the Serb people at that time, and you explained that what you meant here was that Serbs "would not be sitting in their houses waiting to be rounded up, taken to camps, and killed." That's at transcript page 33901 to 02. I take it from this prior evidence that you felt that the Serbs in Rogatica faced a very serious threat at the time from the Muslim side, the threat of destruction and genocide; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: Well, the experience from previous years could not exclude that threat. Nobody knew for a fact that war would happen the way it did. All of us expected that the leadership would manage to agree at the end of the day. It was end of the 20th century, a period when good reasoning should reign among the people. The fact that there were tensions on both sides did not mean that much. We thought that it was a good negotiating position for a final agreement; however, we -- were always afraid that the Muslims would not agree to a compromise. They would look for a maximum and that as a result of that we might be threatened. The previous experience told us that, and we were aware of that. Therefore we were ready, and that doesn't mean that we organised ourselves on the other side to take action. That doesn't mean that we slept fully dressed and we did not wait for them to come and ring our bells. That means that we knew how to protect ourselves based on the information that we had. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said that: "Therefore, we were ready but it doesn't mean that we organised ourselves to take action." What you did do in 1991, Mr. Veselinovic, is, with Dr. Karadzic's support you worked to mobilise the Serbs in Rogatica to deal with that threat that you felt existed from the Muslim side; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: We just wanted to help the legitimate authorities of the state that existed until then to function better. We tried to help the JNA to mobilise people and to be able to carry out all those tasks that were within its purview because Muslims boycotted the JNA, they boycotted mobilisation efforts; Serbs didn't. And I'm not saying and I don't think that the Serbs are the culprits and that our organisation has to take the blame for advising the Serbs to abide by the rules of the then-Yugoslavia and the rules of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Veselinovic, I'm just going to play you an intercepted conversation from September 1991 and then ask you a couple of questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And before it begins, the English is subtitled on the intercept so I don't believe there's any need to translate it. Sorry, this is Exhibit P3406.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Female NN: Yes, can I help you? "Sveto: Tell me, may I talk to Dr. Karadzic? "Female NN: What did you say your name was, Sveto, right? "Sveto: Yes. "Male NN: Hello Sveto. "Sveto: Tell me. "Male NN: Could you wait for just a moment. The doctor is on the other line. "Sveto: Okay. "Male NN: How is it over there towards Visegrad? "Sveto: Well, so-so. "Male NN: Is that so? "Sveto: No, I heard that Serbia is in danger. Serbia is in danger and they won't stop until they reduce it to the size of the Belgrade pashalik. "Male NN: He's about to finish this, he'll be with you in just a moment. "Sveto: Is there anything else? Okay. Thank you. Thank you. Good-bye."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can hear the background conversation but we cannot understand. [Voiceover] "Radovan Karadzic: Thank you. Good-bye. Hello? "Sveto: Good afternoon. "Radovan Karadzic: Good afternoon, Sveto. "Sveto: Doctor, Risto told me to call you. "Radovan Karadzic: We should be in touch all the time. What's the situation up there? "Sveto: Well, so, so. It's God knows what. Those from Han Pijesak, our reservists have taken our positions from Rogatica to Mesici. "Radovan Karadzic: Aha. "Sveto: In Rogatica reserve police forces are getting mobilised. "Radovan Karadzic: Good. "Sveto: We have sent our men to join the reserve forces as well ... "Radovan Karadzic: By all means. "Sveto: So that they don't do something stupid to us, surprise us. "Radovan Karadzic: Absolutely. Definitely. "Sveto: We're ready. We're waiting to see what happens next. "Radovan Karadzic: Can you help Visegrad? "Sveto: We can. "Radovan Karadzic: Do that, get in touch and let them take up positions at Sjemec up there, let them prepare to help Visegrad. Because if they start the war, they'll start it against the people and against the army. "Sveto: Yes, I've already agreed to meet with Brano at Sjemec. "Radovan Karadzic: Aha. Good. It should -- and the column is waiting there. 60 vehicles. Tomorrow the column is going to be enormous. It will take several kilometres to pass through Visegrad because the army won't yield. Are you in touch? Look, Zoran Vujovic can't get through to you at all. Please call him. He said that some man at the number that you had given him would not talk to him. "Sveto: I know nothing about it. "Radovan Karadzic: Who's that? "Sveto: I don't know at all. "Radovan Karadzic: I beg your pardon? "Sveto: Well, I don't know anything either. Me neither ... "Radovan Karadzic: The number you gave out -- "Sveto: He must have taken down the wrong number. "Radovan Karadzic: Aha. You see he may taken the wrong number. Tell me what is your situation. If it is difficult should we send from somewhere else to help you? "Sveto: No, no need for now, no need for right now. At Sjemec, we will prepare it all for helping them if necessary. This evening Brano and I will meet up here. "Radovan Karadzic: Aha, yes, yes. Good. And the police should help too. They'll co-operate with the police for as long as they are treating the military properly. You mustn't do anything against the military. No discussion. The army must pass through Visegrad. "Sveto: Shall we -- "Radovan Karadzic: The army is not going to clean up. They'll destroy Visegrad, they will not give in. So they should know that. "Sveto: Will the military now turn across Sjemec? It's critical down there through the tunnels. "Radovan Karadzic: It's critical through the tunnels, is it. "Sveto: ... eight tunnels. They can place it anywhere ... in the tunnel, destroy the first transporter and block it. "Radovan Karadzic: Aha, good. Call Zoran, call the garrison in Uzice and suggest that they should go across Sjemec. However, they still have to go through Visegrad; right? "Sveto: They don't have to. "Radovan Karadzic: They don't have to, instead ... "Sveto: Via Rogatica, to Ustipraca and Gorazde. "Radovan Karadzic: How come they can't go to Visegrad? Where will they cross the river? "Sveto: Well, in Ustipraca. They're bypassing Visegrad. "Radovan Karadzic: Good. "Sveto: They're bypassing through Medjedja. "Radovan Karadzic: Aha. "Sveto: The Drina canyon. "Radovan Karadzic: Good. And where are they going to cross the Drina River? "Sveto: Across Drina, they'll cross Drina in Ustipraca. It's 12 kilometres between Ustipraca and Gorazde. No tunnels, no attacks. "Radovan Karadzic: So it was him who was shooting from that side of the river, is it? "Sveto: Yes. "Radovan Karadzic: In Rudo, is it? Not Rudo but -- "Sveto: No, no. From Visegrad go across Sjemec, across Borik to Rogatica, and from Rogatica to Gorazde. "Radovan Karadzic: Well, okay, but you have to go through Visegrad? "Sveto: You don't. "Radovan Karadzic: You don't? "Sveto: In fact, you do, yes. "Radovan Karadzic: Well, you have to go through Visegrad. "Sveto: You have to go through Visegrad. "Radovan Karadzic: You secure Visegrad because that's the narrow point, and then the rest, let them decide to go across Sjemec. "Sveto: Yes. "Radovan Karadzic: Get in touch with ... you have to get in touch with the garrison and with this -- and they're looking for you. They cannot get through to you in any way. Is Kusic there somewhere? "Sveto: Doctor, Kusic is down-town somewhere. "Radovan Karadzic: Okay. And where are you? "Sveto: I'm at home at the moment. "Radovan Karadzic: Aha. Come on, please do that and make sure that they provide duty service over there. "Sveto: Everything has been provided as far as it concerns our work. "Radovan Karadzic: And the full, full, full mobility of the party. A full mobility of everything, all the forces that you have, everything you have. If necessary, add the Romanija forces too. "Sveto: Okay, boss. "Radovan Karadzic: All right. "Sveto: All right. Agreed."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic, this person named Sveto calling Dr. Karadzic from Rogatica, that's you; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: My name is Sveto. I'm from Rogatica. Honestly, I forgot about this conversation. I can't remember. Can you help me and tell me the date of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's from the 20th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: Very well. I don't remember. I've heard everything now and I don't see anything in dispute here. What we did was to enable the Yugoslav People's Army to do their work. They were a legitimate army in the state with whose integrity it protected.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Veselinovic, just to be clear, this Sveto is clearly an SDS member because at the end of the intercept Dr. Karadzic says: "And a full, full, full mobility of the party. A full mobility of everything, all the forces that you have, everything you have." And Sveto responds: "Okay, boss." Now, you were the president of the SDS in Rogatica at the time. This Sveto is clearly you talking to Dr. Karadzic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: Most probably, most probably. I'm Sveto from Rogatica. I'm saying I don't remember the details of this conversation; however, I don't see in this conversation what you claim, that President Karadzic sent me a message to kill one-third, to baptise the other third, and to expel the last third --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Veselinovic, the question is whether -- not whether there's anything disputable, but whether you confirm that's you that had a talk with Mr. Karadzic at the time in this intercept. So this Sveto is yourself, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me say that I agree. I'm Sveto from Rogatica. I believe that the voices belong to me and Mr. Karadzic, judging by the timbre of the voice and the way we speak, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And in this conversation, you state that the reserve police forces in Rogatica are getting mobilised. You state that you have sent "our men" to join the reserve forces as well. And then Karadzic, as I noted, orders full mobility of the party, full mobility of everything, all the forces that you have, everything you have. And you say: "Okay, boss." Those are all references to your efforts supported by Dr. Karadzic to mobilise the Serbs in Rogatica to deal with the threat that you consider to be coming from the Muslim side; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: Why are you mentioning Srebrenica? This was in 1991, when Muslims boycotted the calls to come to the manoeuvres of the JNA. Last time I showed you documents in which you could see that, on behalf of the SDS, we invited the Serbian people to respond and come to the manoeuvres of the JNA in Han Pijesak. That unit was deployed there at the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992. One part of that unit was in Sjemec and the other part was in the brigade. So there's nothing in dispute here. We invited the Serbs to accept the boycott of the response to join the JNA because when the Muslims boycotted the JNA and did not want to join the manoeuvres, there was a --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic --

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: -- fear that if the Serbs responded and joined the manoeuvres, the villages would remain empty.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are a lot of problems with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic, I'd like to move on now to 1992. The Chamber has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You -- does it mean that you have difficulty with the transcript or there's a translation issue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am now reconnected. Things are not being recorded. A lot of things are not recorded. The Prosecutor did not mention "Srebrenica," however, the witness received the word "Srebrenica" in interpretation. On page 5, line 10, he said: We learned from the experiences of 1941. And now page 12, line 11, it should read that the Serbian villages would remain empty. There was a fear that the Serbian villages would remain empty. This should be recorded on line 11 -- I can see that this was indeed repeated. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it appears in line 12 and 13 -- 13 and 14 and that's when you interrupted. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic, the Chamber has received evidence from numerous witnesses including Mile Ujic, who was the artillery co-ordinator for the Rogatica Brigade, that on the 22nd of May, 1992, the Rogatica Brigade conducted a major shelling attack on Muslim-populated parts of the municipality, referred to at transcript page 33460. Now, you don't deny that that attack took place, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, objection, Mr. President. Mr. President, since this witness is now testifying for the second time, it's our position that the cross-examination should not be allowed to go back over issues that were part of his original testimony or that were within the scope of his original testimony, but should be limited to the statement allegedly made by KDZ051 or any issues relating to credibility as to whether or not that statement was made. But to go and rehash the events in Rogatica with this witness I would suggest is not proper.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm really focused on paragraphs 6 and 7 of the witness's statement, where he makes some broad assertions about his conclusions as to Dr. Karadzic's views and policies. I am dealing with that through a number of steps. I will conclude by addressing that directly, but I'm building up to that and I could go into it further, but I'm reluctant to do so in front of the witness. I could do that in more detail, if you wish, if the witness would be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your submission is while you agree with Mr. Robinson's observation in principle, but you are dealing with paragraphs 6 and 7 --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- of this revised -- new statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll allow you to continue. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Veselinovic, you don't deny that the Rogatica Brigade on the 22nd of May, 1992, conducted a major shelling attack on Muslim-populated parts of the municipality, do you?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said in my last statement. As far as I remember, 22nd May was the day when the Muslim forces killed a Serb, Drazen Mihajlovic, and that was the day the conflict began. They did not let the body of the dead man be collected, and that was the day when our president of the Crisis Staff made contact with them. And they said when after that man they kill another ten Serbs, only then would they allow the bodies to be retrieved. An operation was launched to get that body back. I don't know what Mile Ujic did, but I believe that was the day when a clash occurred between the two sides and there were losses - I don't know if only on one side or on both. That's when all contact between the Serb and Muslim sides ceased and general chaos began. And the initial reason was precisely the murder of Drazen Mihajlovic on that day, 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You're not really answering my question. You said that an operation was launched to get that body back, referring to the body of Mihajlovic. That operation involved shelling Muslim-populated parts of the municipality. You must have remembered that, there was a major shelling attack. You must have seen it or heard it or at least heard of it; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: I remember that. I remember that. I remember the murder of Drazen Mihajlovic, which caused a massive conflict between the two sides, whether it was on that day or the following day, the Serb forces did retrieve the body of Mihajlovic. How? I don't know. I don't know in what way they did that. I was not involved in those operations. I was never involved in combat during the whole war. All I know about it is what Mile Ujic told me. And I'm not a military expert to be able to explain to you here whether there was shelling and how many shells were fired from a 72- or 92-mortar, what weapons were artillery weapons or otherwise. All I know is that that's when the fighting began.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And the Chamber has also heard evidence that these attacks on Muslim areas in Rogatica during the summer of 1992, caused Muslims living in those places to flee. And I refer to KDZ607, P3289, paragraphs 11 and 12; and Mile Ujic again at 33466 to 33467. Now, you must have known that large numbers of Muslims were fleeing their homes and villages from these attacks; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wonder if the question should be put that way, enumerating exhibits. Why not show them to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, the references are for the parties and the Court. The question's fair.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was shelled was the area where the soldier Mihajlovic had been killed. Now, to what extent there were Muslim villages there, there probably were some, but at that time there were no Serbs left in town either. It was divided. On one side, the Serb population was concentrated; on the other side were Muslims. At that time, there were already refugees from the area of Gorazde --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic, I'm going to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: -- and in other towns chaos had reigned for some time already --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm interrupting you because you're not responding to my question. Are you telling me that you were unaware of the fact that Muslims during the summer of 1992 were fleeing their homes and villages which were being attacked by the army? You're totally unaware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: The army did not attack Muslim villages without any reason. The army was fighting Muslim military forces. I don't know what you're trying to put to me. Are you trying to say that Muslims were living peacefully and then some Serbs came and shelled them and opened fire at them? There were Muslim forces in Muslim villages in Muslim areas and Serb forces were in Serb areas. After that murder a clash started. On one side Serbs whenever defeated would flee from their areas, and in the town itself there were no Serbs left, although it had been a 60 per cent Serb town, full of Serb houses. And after that clash, the Muslims started leaving their areas. I'm not saying they didn't, and I said in my previous statement that at that time I spoke to the refugees, I was the first to come into town to inspect abandoned housing, and that I accommodated --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic --

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: -- Serb refugees from Gorazde in those abandoned houses --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm interrupting you again because you're moving away from the question, and if I could ask you to please focus on my questions as precisely as you can. Okay. The Chamber's also received a great deal of evidence of Serb soldiers capturing, detaining, and expelling Muslim civilians from Rogatica. And I would refer, for example, to the evidence of Bazdar at P3286, page 4; Pasic, P59, pages 860 to 875; Mr. Hurko, P3267, paragraphs 14 to 22; and Mr. Isakovic, P127, pages 4 to 5. You were aware that that was happening at the time?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: I don't know what evidence you have before this Court, but I'm telling you it's not the way you are describing it. There was a war. There was fighting against the Muslim army. Muslim soldiers were being captured, they were being fired at. Areas were being mopped up from their army. They launched attacks, we launched counter-attacks. So it's absolutely not the lop-sided way you are trying to get me to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we have P6153, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic, this is a Drina Corps report to the Eastern Bosnian Corps command, containing a list of captured persons of Muslim ethnicity in the areas of Rogatica, Visegrad, Rudo, Cajnice, and Foca. And you can see that the first list pertains to Rogatica, and I think you would agree with me that the first 16 names on this list are all Muslim women; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes, Muslim names, women's names.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, a moment ago you claimed that -- when I put to you that Muslim civilians were being detained, you said Muslim soldiers were being captured. Now, you don't contend seriously that these Muslim women, most of whom were elderly and, in fact, one of them was 101 years old at the time, were Muslim soldiers, do you?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: I'm not contending they were soldiers, but they probably happened to be in a combat zone. They were probably -- I mean, both sides, when they were fighting, they were fighting in their own villages where women and children also lived. When you enter an area, it's quite natural that you will find all sorts of people there, the soldiers and non-combatants, and soldiers who had simply cast away their weapons and dressed as civilians. And of course, you would remove the civilians to protect them from further conflict. I don't know what was going on here. I had no contact with the corps, with the army. I don't know about the fate of these civilians or why they were arrested. But the fact is there was no front line here, no proper front line where there would be only army troops holding positions and fighting. The war was being waged in villages where there were women and children and the elderly. These women must have been evacuated from a combat zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said you didn't know what was going on here, you had no contact with the corps. You are probably aware that in recent years, the Bosnian state court has convicted a number of members of the Rogatica Brigade for killing, detaining, expelling, and mistreating Muslims in Rogatica. And I refer to P6106, P6107, and D1665. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that and all the people from Rogatica who had been convicted, I know about that. I know what they had been charged with, what they were convicted for. Those were individual crimes they had committed and they were judged for them. Of course they should not have done that, and as far as I know, they did not have orders to do that from superior commands, especially not from President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we go to P988, please. And I'd like page 68 of the English and page 87 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is approximately -- if you could look approximately two-thirds of the way down the page in the B/C/S and right at the bottom of the page in English. Mr. Veselinovic, this is a transcript from the 28th of August, 1995, Assembly and it's Dr. Karadzic speaking. And approximately two-thirds of the way down the page he says: "To tell the truth, there are towns that we grabbed for ourselves and there were only 30 per cent of us ..." And if we could turn the page in the English. "I can name as many of those as you want, but we cannot give up the towns where we made up 70 per cent. Don't let this get around, but remember how many of us there were in Bratunac, how many in Srebrenica, how many in Visegrad, how many in Rogatica, how many in Vlasenica, in Zvornik, et cetera. Due to strategic importance, they had to become ours, and no one is practically questioning it anymore ..." Now, when Dr. Karadzic says "don't let this get around but remember how many of us there were in" places including Rogatica, he's referring to the dramatic demographic transformation in these areas? And in fact, the Serbs used to be a minority in Rogatica and these other places, but that's no longer the case in August of 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: If I look at the entire municipality of Rogatica, there were about 40 per cent Serbs, I think, but if we separate from Rogatica Zepa, which at that time had 6- to 7.000 population and which remained all the way up to 1995 an area controlled by the Muslim forces, that Zepa, when we separate it from the total population, considerably increases the population numbers in the municipality of Rogatica. So if we take Zepa away, the ethnic composition in Rogatica would be half/half between Serbs and Muslims. And Zepa is an area that belongs to Rogatica municipality, but when you cross Sjemec and Borika you get to Zepa and it's in a valley closer to the Drina River and before the war it didn't have even a paved road. There was a macadam road that connected it --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic --

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: -- with Rogatica and with the Visegrad area. There's the Drina River area separating it from Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic, this speech is made on the 28th of August, 1995, Zepa had fallen. There were no more Muslims left in Zepa and there were certainly no -- very few Muslims left in the remainder of the municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes, when this Assembly session took place there were very few Muslims. In fact, there were almost none in Rogatica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when Dr. Karadzic says: "Due to strategic importance they had to become ours ..." and he includes Rogatica in that list, he is connecting the demographic transformation to the strategic importance of these places; in other words, the demographic transformation of Rogatica ensured the Bosnian Serb leadership's hold on this strategically important municipality. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: That's a fact. The Serbian leadership remained in power in Rogatica. Now, what Dr. Karadzic understood by strategically important, probably cutting off that green transversal, the connection with Sandzak, and separating Serb people on the one side of the Drina and the Serbs on the other side of the Drina, meaning in Serbia, then Yugoslavia. But if we add up all the areas, Rogatica, Visegrad, Foca, Srebrenica, the total population was less than the number of Serbs in Sarajevo. And in 1995, there was not a single Serb in Sarajevo. So the war had brought about shifts of population, that's a fact. The territories controlled by Serbs at that time were mono-ethnic and the areas controlled by the Muslims were mono-ethnic Muslim and there were no Serbs in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Veselinovic, that was no accident, was it? The acts of the Rogatica Brigade in 1992, the killings, the expulsions, the mistreatment, those acts furthered Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership's policy to transform the demographics of Rogatica, the strategically important municipality in their eyes, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: That's what you think. I'm telling you again, there was a war going on. On one side there were Serbs who wanted to preserve the existing state of Yugoslavia. On the other side, the idea of the Muslims was to create their own state, to secede from Yugoslavia, and such two different concepts, such diverging concepts, led to the break-up of Yugoslavia. The Muslims did not want to agree to anything, which is proven by the fact that Izetbegovic reneged on his signature on the Lisbon Agreement and the Serbs took power in that municipality. In some other municipalities, the Muslims took power. I cannot accept it when you say that Muslims were the only ones who tortured, killed, and expulsed. No, it's not the way it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Veselinovic. I have nothing further. However, I'd just -- I don't know whether it was a mistake in the translation or whether you misspoke. But the last line says: "I cannot accept it when you say that Muslims were the only ones who tortured, killed, and expelled" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apologies, it was Serbs. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: Welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Veselinovic, on page 22 it was put to you that the Serb side wanted to re-design the ethnic picture of Rogatica. Can you tell us, was there any talk about establishing the Serb municipality of Rogatica and the Muslim municipality of Rogatica, and that Muslims were able to keep their villages and their parts of the town --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any negotiations about creating two municipalities?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: That's what I testified when I was here last time. We had invested huge efforts in resolving the problems in Rogatica so as to avoid conflict. Our idea was to divide the municipality into Serb and Muslim parts only by administrative lines so that two municipalities would operate side by side until the end of the conflict. The Muslims had agreed to that. We had been working on that, and we had even shown a map here depicting this division of the territory that had been verified by our common Assembly, where the Muslim deputies were in the majority. Great efforts had been made, but they were later annulled by the Muslim leadership who had forbidden local Muslims to continue negotiating with us. And then Izetbegovic, withdrawing his signature from the Lisbon Agreement, put an end to our efforts on the local level to divide the municipality and avoid conflict. So there were no pressures from the Serb side. There was no intention to make Rogatica a purely Serb area where there would be no Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us -- can you tell us about your career, where did you work?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: Before the war I worked in the municipal administration of social revenues as a member of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the personal income of employees recorded somewhere? Was there a payroll?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes, like in every organisation, every enterprise. There were log-books of personal incomes for every employee, and every month the salary of every employee would be recorded against his names, including all the contributions and withdrawals.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness 1D49037 without broadcasting it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what it is that we have in front of us, and does this have to do with KDZ051? What's the year? What's the month?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not sure what these -- where this line of questioning is exactly heading, but I don't think it has anything to do with the cross-examination. I didn't mention KDZ051 at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Excellencies, everything here is based on the false testimony of KDZ051, and that's why we called this witness because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You should have raised it in your direct examination, not in your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I got this document during the cross-examination. I got it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow. You got it during your cross-examination -- during cross-examination of Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the municipality sent this. I got it just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow -- I don't understand, Mr. Karadzic. Municipality sent it while Ms. Gustafson was cross-examining this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that they sent it during my examination but it arrived later on. You see, it doesn't even have an ERN number. It is a completely new document, fresh. I didn't receive it before the cross started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If Mr. Robinson could assist us in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I think our case manager got this document this morning before the examination started and we told him to put it in e-court, and it's possible that Dr. Karadzic didn't see it until the examination began. And I would agree that it doesn't arise from the cross-examination and I would also point out that I'm struggling to find out the relevance of the entire cross-examination when the witness was brought here to testify about the statement of this witness and -- of KDZ051. And there's no charge of genocide in Rogatica even in the indictment. So the only relevant information should be concerning whether this statement was made and it seems to me that the Prosecution has not contested that in the least bit that the witness never made such a statement, they never alluded to anybody who saw him at the school where the witness was, they never alluded to anyone who ever heard him repeat such things. And so the cross-examination doesn't contest the basic elements of the statement. That being said, I don't think that Dr. Karadzic needs to use this document either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Mr. Karadzic, please move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one question, Mr. Veselinovic. Do you happen to know from what time and from what country this formula of three-thirds stems from, one-third should be killed, one-third should be baptised, and one-third should be expelled?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC [Re-called]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I researched this on the internet. 1882, Russia, when Russians were expelling Jews and it was revived with the slogan: Serbs should be hanged on willow trees in the Ustasha regime. And Mile Budak, who was a minister in the Independent State of Croatia in 1941, he launched that slogan. And under that slogan, only in Jasenovac over 600.000 Serbs were killed as well as Jews and Roma. So the slogan which is shameful for the Serbs, no Serb would ever use it as their motto because we know full well and we felt this on our own skin, all the horrors of that slogan. If before our judiciary any witness were to mention what this witness said, believe me, they would have just laughed because there is no way the Serbs could have used anything that meant the mass killing of Serbs during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Mr. Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your second testimony, Mr. Veselinovic. Thank you again for your coming to The Hague to give it. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's an issue with respect to an exhibit number from the Registry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D49025 receives Exhibit Number D4193, under seal. My apologies, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic is ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. While he's coming in, I apologise to the Trial Chamber, the fact that he wasn't ready on the last week was completely my fault. I had omitted him from the production schedule that I had sent -- the last one that I had sent to the Victims and Witnesses Section. So that's -- it wasn't their fault at all that he wasn't brought, but it was mine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacevic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Kovacevic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to remind myself and you to pause between our questions and answers. Also, let us speak slowly so that our sentences would be recorded in the transcript. Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D9542 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that statement of yours on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Last page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the last page please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. This is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team? Are there any inaccuracies that should be changed?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Basically it is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers be the same as those contained in this statement?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, basically they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement according to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number D4194, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out in the English language a summary of Mr. Sveto Kovacevic's statement. [In English] Sveto Kovacevic was elected president of the Celinac Municipal Assembly. He was a member of the SDS since the formation of the municipal board in Celinac in June 1990 and a member of the Main Board since the SDS Assembly on 12th of July, 1991. The key programme goals of the SDS were the preservation of Yugoslavia and the equality of the Serbian people in BH. The SDS leadership was in favour of resolving political issues through agreement between political representatives of all the peoples. The SDS adopted a decision to freeze the work of the party from May 1992 to February 1993. The work was renewed at the Jahorina plenum, when it was decided that all the organs of the SDS should step up activity in order to strengthen national unity and prevent any form of extremism. After frequent abuse of voting system by the coalition of Muslims and Croats, the culmination of the imposition of their will was the decision to call a referendum for a sovereign and independent BH. On April the 4th, 1992, the Rump Presidency of BH declared the mobilisation of its military and paramilitary formations and formed Crisis Staffs at the different levels. Later, Crisis Staffs were also formed in a number of municipalities and local communes under Serbian control. President Karadzic was the key man in the peace process and insisted on the respect of laws. President Karadzic never uttered a single word at any of the sessions which referred to crimes, nor signed any decisions to commit a crime against anyone. When several Muslim houses were torched in the municipality of Celinac, Dr. Karadzic immediately took interest in whether the perpetrators had been brought to justice. The Municipal Assembly of Celinac was constituted on 19th of December, 1990. Since less than 10 per cent of the population of Celinac municipality was Muslims, the SDS could have formed the municipal government independently, but decided not to do so and the composition of the Municipal Assembly was based on the election results. Life in the municipality from 1990 to 1992 was as difficult for the majority Serbian as for the other two nationalities. In order to deal with the problems that most affected the population, the Crisis Staff was formed in May 1992. The Crisis Staff was independent and did not receive any instructions from the SDS leadership. The first major incident in Celinac happened in August 1992, when a group of Serbs started riots in response to the killing of a group of Serbian soldiers of the Celinac Brigade at the Vlasic front. Several houses were set on fire and, as a consequence, the Muslims expressed their wish to leave the municipality. Mr. Kovacevic managed to calm the situation and to keep them in their homes and did so by informing the police and by declaring a curfew. All the participants in the torching, killings, and riots were arrested and brought to trial. The founding Assembly of the community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina was held on 25th of April, 1991, in Celinac. Representatives of the SDS, SDA, and HDZ of Bosanska Krajina were also invited as well as the opposite parties. After several months, the community of municipalities was renamed the Autonomous Region of Krajina. The leadership in Pale did not have any influence on the formation of the ARK. President Karadzic was not in favour of the formation of the ARK. He did not attend a single session in the ARK, and he did not have an influence on any decisions that the ARK took. The civilian authorities at the republican, regional, and municipal levels did not support, plan, incite, order, or aid the permanent removal of Bosnian Muslims and Croats from the territory of BH which the Serbs claimed for themselves. [Interpretation] I would just like to put one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, did you fully take part in creating the policy of the Serb Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I took part in creating the policy of the Serb Democratic Party. If you allow me a digression here, as for the founding Assembly, it wasn't that people were just invited; they were invited and they attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the founding Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The founding Assembly that I chaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who carried out the policy of the Serb Democratic Party in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In my municipality, the programme of the Serb Democratic Party was carried out by the municipal board of the Serb Democratic Party and I as a member of the Main Board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kovacevic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in most part in writing, that is -- that is, through your written statement. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, I see you have a number of papers in front of you. Could you please put them to one side, and if you need to refer to them, can you please ask the Trial Chamber's permission to do that.

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I don't need it at all. I took a CD, too, just in case, from the founding Assembly, but I see -- well, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You added a paragraph to your statement which is paragraph 43, and it makes reference to Exhibit P2638 and that's the decision on the status of the non-Serbian population of Celinac municipality issued on the 23rd of July, 1992. You make a couple of points in relation to that. You say that you weren't the municipal president on that date and that all of the restrictions listed in the decision related to the 34 individuals mentioned in Article 2. So first dealing with the restrictions relating to these individuals, let's just examine the document, shall we.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have Exhibit P2638 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking at Article 1, you agree that on a plain reading of this article that it states that due to combat operations in Celinac municipality and further afield special status is given to the non-Serbian population of Celinac municipality?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Could I have the last page with the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, this exhibit here in the B/C/S, it is not very clear, the very end of the document. And I can take you to another version of the document which is much clearer and we can see the bottom of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But do you have your statement, Mr. Kovacevic, witness statement given to Mr. Karadzic's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's D04194.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand that. I have my witness statement in front of me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, yes. She was referring to paragraph 43 of your statement. So if necessary, you may take a look at your statement, paragraph 43.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there is no need to do that. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'm not saying with any certainty that I signed this, but I'm not avoiding it all together. I hadn't handed over until that point in time. Now, what is all of this about? This decision was written only for the sake of security. Actually, 34 persons who are mentioned here were known to the police from before. Now, what does that mean? That means that these are people who were prone to different kinds of excessive behaviour, incidents, and so on. We at the Crisis Staff assessed that these persons should not be punished at all. I'm talking about misdemeanours proceedings. Quite simply, we thought that they should be placed under control in order to preserve their lives, and after a brief period of time we would return them so that they could go on living together with us as they had before. This decision was in force for a very short period of time and it turned out to be very good and very wise. After that, all the people who saw that - and I'm talking about ethnic Muslims - they came to me and they said that it was very wise, very smart. All of these people are alive and healthy, they are living and working in Celinac, except for natural deaths that occurred in the meantime --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you haven't answered my question. I said: Looking at Article 1 on page 1, you agree that a plain reading of this article states that it -- special status is given to the non-Serbian population of Celinac municipality. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but under these circumstances because we are talking about --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: -- a period that was 20 years ago --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- you've answered --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Looking at Article 2, it lists 34 citizens which are given "a different status from other non-Serb inhabitants." If we go over the page.

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Not 36, 34. Secondly, I explained in great detail what the reason was, for the sake of safety and security, because we managed to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: -- keep all of these people alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't want you to --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: -- they're alive to this day --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting. I don't want you to keep repeating what you've previously said. I simply wanted you to agree that Article 2 lists 34 citizens which are given a different status from other non-Serb inhabitants; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What does it say under the 34th name: "These are persons considered who have previously acted negatively and compromised themselves in various ways, thereby harming the Serbian people, on account of which they are given a different status from other non-Serb inhabitants." That's what it states in the document, doesn't it? Does it state that in the document or not, Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Can I read Article 2, please, word for word?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. No, excuse me, you can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be zoomed in, please? It says as follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- have been assessed as persons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So this is Article 2 on page 1 of the document, it's listing the names. If we can go to page -- that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It then says because these people have been considered negatively against the Serbian population, they are given a different status from other non-Serb inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It's not a status. It's protection. It depends on the choice of words and what the typists typed up, but this is a classical type of protection, nothing bad ever happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Right. Looking at Article 3 - if we can have the English back on the screen, please - Article 3 makes reference to citizens from Article 1; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Article 4 specifically refers to the citizens from Article 1; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Article 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Specifically refers to citizens from Article 1?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: But only on a voluntary basis and you can read it yourself. It's very clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And by that you're referring to this permits citizens only to leave in an organised fashion with their entire family and with necessary documentation. That's what you were just referring to, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Only those who wanted. There was no coercion at all --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacevic --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: -- the authorities --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to go through this document. Article 5, if we can go to Article 5, once again the citizens from Article 1; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this article is very specific about what the citizens from Article 1 shall not do, which include moving around town between 4.00 p.m. and 6.00 a.m. the following morning, travelling outside their village or communicating with relatives outside the municipality, lingering on the streets or gathering in groups of more than three people, selling or exchanging property, driving cars, hunting, fishing, or swimming in the rivers. And that's specifically what the citizens from Article 1 are forbidden from doing; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that was actually the protection of the entire population, to prevent them from being involved in incidents. People who came from front lines on furlough to visit their families, for burials, were prone to causing incidents. We were afraid that somebody would get killed, that some harm would happen to them. And when we analysed the situation, we made the decision, the decision was in force for a very short time, and eventually it proved to be very wise because it served a purpose. The population was indeed protected.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So I think you've just said that this decision related -- that this decision related to the entire non-Serb population and not just the 34 individuals in Article 2; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: If we read the entire decision, it referred to only 34 people in this part and the rest was after 1600 hours. It is very clear. I don't have to explain, do I?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, we will continue reading the document then. Article 6 is very specific about what the citizens from Article 1 are obliged to do; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Article 7, it's specifically directed at the 34 people named in Article 2, and that they are additionally forbidden from - if we can go over to page 4 in the English - "making any contact whatsoever with people in the neighbourhood or further afield or making any kind of movement between 0000 hours and 2400 hours, except when called for work obligation."

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you're saying. The question is not clear at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your assertion that this document only applies to the 34 named persons in Article 2 isn't supported by a plain reading of the document, because as I've just taken you to Article 7 it says, specifically directed at the 34 names in Article 2, that Article, every other article, so Article 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 all refer to citizens from Article 1. Article 1 defines those citizens as the non-Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so then Article 7 is saying, in addition to these things, these 34 people which are listed are also additionally forbidden to do X and Y. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can see that. That was the decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at eight past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I please introduce Rafaela Steffen Goncalves da Rosa, who is from Brazil and is studying for a masters at the University of Tilburg. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sutherland. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, I want to deal very quickly with the second point that you make in this new paragraph, paragraph 43, that you weren't the municipality president on the 23rd of July, 1992. I just have a few mechanics about what goes on in Municipal Assembly meetings. Minutes are taken as a regular course of business; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Will you allow me to say something about the previous decision? I would like to say just one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, I would like you to answer my question, please. Minutes, are they taken as a regular course of business, the -- at the Municipal Assembly meetings?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I did not tell you one very important sentence about this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please go on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, with all due respect to the Prosecutor's questions, I claim that those Muslims, i.e., non-Serbs, experienced any persecution or sanctions. The contrary is true and this can be confirmed by the people who were on the list. It was a positive decision and many are still grateful for it, and it is the Muslims who will tell you that. Don't just take my words for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, now can we get back to the minutes taken at a regular -- of the Municipal Assembly. They're taken, are they not, at each meeting?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me whether minutes of the meetings were taken, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And at the Celinac Municipal Assembly meetings, the minute-taker was Marica Vujatovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And she was your secretary?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 25778, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, these are minutes taken by your secretary, yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I need to read this. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What you're seeing on page 1 is the minutes of the 15th Session of the Celinac Municipal Assembly held on the 31st of March, 1992. Do you recognise your secretary's handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that it's hers. I really did not study her handwriting because what I received from her was in a printed form.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to the -- page 22, please, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I should look at the agenda first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And it's page 15 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you see at the bottom of the page her signature? Do you see there, Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I can't say anything before I look at the agenda. I don't know what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: These are the minutes of the meeting held on the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to the following page, please, in the B/C/S, that's page 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We see here this is the minutes of the 16th Assembly Session on the 13th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to page 42 in the B/C/S and page 29 of the English --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did not show me the agenda. Only the agenda would jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, if you look at this -- this is the 28th of July, 1992, maybe this will jog your memory. This is the --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: But I can only see the first item of the agenda, which cannot jog my memory, because where it says "adopting the minutes of the former session," it doesn't really mean much to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Her question is whether you recognise the passage which says the minutes were taken by Marica Vujatovic. Do you remember Marica Vujatovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Another question is whether you recognise her handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recognise her handwriting because I received materials in a typed form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. You see there, Mr. Kovacevic, under where it says the minutes were taken by Marica Vujatovic, the session was chaired by the SO, and the SO -- the acronym for SO is Municipal Assembly, is it not? The session was chaired by the SO President, Sveto Kovacevic, who proposed the following agenda for this session. So do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary, we can show him the next page, which lists the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we go to the following page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you see the agenda there, Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us go back to the page -- the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, these minutes have you chairing the session as the Municipal Assembly President on the 28th of July, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I chaired every session while I was in office. There's no doubt about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, in paragraph 43 of your statement you say when this decision that we just went through before the break on the -- which was issued on the 23rd of July, 1992, you said: I was not the municipal president on the date this document was issued. And I've just taken you to the minutes which show you chairing this session. So you were still the president at that time, yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: If you understood me properly, let me repeat the same words in that same order. I said that at that moment I didn't sign -- or, rather, I cannot guarantee that I signed it, but that was indeed my period. That's what I said. I did not say the way you want to put it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload the document, his witness statement, Exhibit D4194, paragraph 43, last page. Do you have your statement, Mr. Kovacevic, witness statement? Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Paragraph 43.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is what it says, but you asked me if I had signed this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the question -- wait for the question. So second sentence in paragraph 43 is not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I told you here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, I'm asking -- I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when I first arrived here -- but here effectively I can't say anything else because in the documents it says that I had joined Metal. I can't state anything differently because I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Please hear the question. My question is whether this second sentence of this paragraph is correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, if we're talking about the document, I have the originals of the documents testifying to my transfer. The document says that I wasn't. However, I had not handed over my duties, which is why I would be there from time to time and that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have 65 ter number 25778 back on the screen, please. If we could go to page 47 of the B/C/S and page 31 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, this is the minutes of the 17th Session, again called the 17th Session, held on the 5th of August and that's because on the 28th of July, a quorum couldn't be reached, which we saw a moment ago, when the document was up on the screen. So the 17th Session is reconvened to the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to the following page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And it says there - the minutes again taken by your secretary - the session was chaired by the Municipal Assembly President Sveto Kovacevic. So you're still the president on the 5th of August, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It is just like I explained a while ago. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And as president of the War Presidency, this decision that we looked at before the break, Exhibit P02638 on restrictions for the non-Serb population, it was issued under your name; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 29 that the Muslim population remained throughout the war and to this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 00242R, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is the 1991 census data, and it says there that Celinac population of Muslims was 1.446 and there were 76 Croats. Do you see that there on the right-hand side of the document?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now I'd like to call up 65 ter number 25785, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And just before the document goes off the screen we can see that there's 16.554 Serbs. This document is from SNB Banja Luka, April 1993 figures, and it states in this document that there are 1.120 Muslims in 1991, but we know from the document we've just looked at that it was closer to 1.450; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
