utterances.text: If you read that document carefully, it also contains categories "Others" and "Yugoslavs." A certain number of Muslims and a certain number of Croats and a certain number of Serbs declared themselves as "Yugoslavs." What I know is that in the entire municipality there were about 1700 or 1750 of them. It's not an exact number but it's approximately that number, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we can see here that in April 1993 there's only 770 Muslims inhabitants in Celinac municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That's not a document, it's not for the centre of the security services to say how many people there are. The valid document for this kind of discussion is the first one we saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a document compiled by the SNB Banja Luka on information that they must have received, and by -- so it states there that almost half the Muslim population have moved out by April 1993, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. Only a part of the population of Memici and Vasici were moved out. In fact, it's one part of the hamlet called Popovac that we returned to them after the incidents. As far as this document is concerned, which is headed the centre of security services, you have to ask them, not me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. The witness hasn't confirmed anything about the document and it's not -- there's no sufficient foundation for its admission through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'll move on. Could I have Exhibit P05449, please. Although, Your Honour, if I can just add on this document here, 65 ter 25785, it's a document that appears to be a document created by the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I thought you were withdrawing that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, we'll not admit this document through this witness. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have Exhibit P05449, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we have it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this is the wrong document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is wrong. What we had was 5549.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I need P5449, please. This document is the 1995 figures comparing them against the 1991 figures by the RDB in Banja Luka. And if we can go to page 3 of the B/C/S/ and the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: For Celinac we can see in 1995 that, in fact, 190 Muslims remain in the municipality and 15 Croats. So your assertion that the Muslim population remained throughout the war and to this day is incorrect, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly correct. I don't rule out that some young people went away to be schooled elsewhere, then that some other people moved out for other reasons. I had a Muslim neighbour whose two children both left, one for Sarajevo, one for Zenica, so it was some sort of natural selection. That anybody was moved out in any other way is certainly untrue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: A natural selection that -- where you have a 1991 figure, even looking at this document of 1.440 Muslims, and in 1991 and in 1995 we're down to -- for the Muslims and Croats combined to 205 people, are you saying that over 1200 just went for schooling, for other reasons, that they simply left their homes, their positions, their lives that they'd built, just because they wanted to move away?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Your contentions are nowhere near being correct. 1995, this is an evaluation from the Ministry of the Interior. They did not make a census nor did they make any real evaluation, so it's not a valid document. I'm telling you again with all certainty that people still live there, they work. Maybe some of them left for university elsewhere or for some other reasons, looking for better living conditions or other reasons. To this day Serbs and Muslims are leaving for economic reasons. But what you are trying to put to me, that they left for some other reasons or moved out for some other reasons, that's really not true. They had genuine protection --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: -- no matter what kind of population they were, they had genuine protection from the authorities of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- in paragraph 29 you say that the population in Celinac didn't have any particular problems. In June 1992, four Muslim businesses were blown up, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, tell me which.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 2 -- I'm sorry. Could I have 65 ter number 257 -- I'm sorry, 65 ter number 25783.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a Radio Banja Luka report about the four Muslim businesses being blown up in Celinac.

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. This is not a document. This is from Radio Banja Luka. They also wrote about me in the newspapers and said on the radio that I had hidden my son from going to high school, whereas my son was actually in the fifth grade of elementary school. It's certainly not true that we did not prosecute perpetrators. Whatever happened, perpetrators were prosecuted and punished. I'm telling you with full responsibility and with great certainty --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: -- they said about my son --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: -- that I had hidden him from doing his military service when he was in the fifth grade of elementary school --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you're repeating yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, objection. First of all, the witness hasn't been able to confirm anything about the document; and secondly, I just wonder about the provenance of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- document, given that there are handwritten alterations to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can -- we'll give an opportunity after hearing him out. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked the witness whether he -- I put it to him that four Muslim businesses were blown up in Celinac and he said: No, no. Now, I've shown him a document which -- which specifically states that four Muslim businesses were blown up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I absolutely see the point. But what is your response to the point raised by Mr. Robinson, i.e., provenance and the authenticity, in light of the fact that there is also handwriting revision -- handwritten revision?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has said that it's a Banja Luka Radio broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It -- he read the title. He didn't confirm that it was broadcast or whatever. We can MFI it until we are satisfied with the provenance or the authenticity of the document, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This document was seized from [sic] the Office of the Prosecutor from the Banja Luka Radio station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless the Defence agrees, you are not giving testimony, so we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives MFI P6576, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, also at this time the mosque in Celinac was attacked, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The non-Serb population posed no threat to the security of the overwhelming Serb population in Celinac municipality, did they?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. We respected that and we did everything to protect that population.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The non-Serb population, though, posed no threat to the security of the Serbian population; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. They posed no threat to the security of the Serbian population, and we appreciated that and we did everything to protect them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you note in paragraphs 17 and 25 of your statement the torching of Muslim houses in Samac village and in Basici [Realtime transcript read in error "Vasici"] sometime later and the intimidation of Muslim population in the villages of Popovac, Basici and Memici. This intimidation included killings, yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Allow me to explain. Memici and Basici are hamlets of Popovac village, which is about 12, 13 kilometres from the centre of Celinac. In those hamlets, Basici and Memici, there were mostly Muslims. And another enclave that had Muslim majority was in Celinac itself. It's true that there was torching in Memici and Basici. It's true that that happened and there were a couple of killings too. And having found out about that, the authorities of the Republika Srpska and the municipal authorities did everything, perhaps not immediately but quickly, to prosecute the perpetrators. I believe one of them is still serving his sentence. They were imprisoned initially in the centre of the security services in Banja Luka and the police station in Celinac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The transcript says "Vasici," but, in fact, you and I both said "Basici." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct, Basici, Basici and Memici --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: -- hamlets of Popovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Inhabitants from the village of Bastici were also killed and Muslim houses set on fire; correct? Now, Bastici is close to Mehovci and Basici, but it is actually in the municipality of Banja Luka. It's a very short distance over the --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. I'll repeat: Basici and Memici belonged to Popovac village, which is in Celinac municipality. And they are 12 to 14 kilometres away from the centre of Celinac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Bastici is in what municipality?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Celinac municipality. It's a hamlet - I'm repeating for the third time - it's a hamlet of Popovac village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. Are you -- and you agree people were killed there and Muslim houses were set on fire?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: You said that it was torched entirely. No. It's true there was an incident, that several houses were set on fire, that several people were killed, and it's true that the authorities responded. When I say "the authorities," I mean the republic and municipal authorities, all these structures. All these people, the perpetrators --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: -- of that unfortunate incident were found --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- I'm sorry to interrupt but you're repeating yourself and I have very, very limited time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I 65 ter number 04210, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report from the 1st Krajina Corps and we see down at the bottom number 3, the situation report, in Bastici village, in the Celinac municipality, five Muslims were killed, two women and three men aged between 16 and 52, Muslims houses were set on fire, and there was shooting in the village of Samac. This is what you were referring to a moment ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Did you say point 3?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if we can turn to the second page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is what you were referring to a moment ago, weren't you, Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I have to clarify one thing. The place called Samac is almost in the centre of Celinac. We should not mix things up. The hamlets of Basici and Memici, although some people called it Sainovici, they are 14 kilometres away from Celinac. And it's true that this incident really happened as described here in the text, and it's true that the authorities did their utmost, most energetically, to take the measures and prosecute perpetrators. And in the end they were convicted and sentenced to many years' imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6577, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 16, 17, and 28 of your statement that these perpetrators were arrested immediately after the acts were committed, they were brought to trial and, as far as you remember, sentenced to 18 years' imprisonment, and you've said it again this morning. Are you referring there to the --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you referring there to the Sugic brothers?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am referring to the brothers whose name I don't want to mention for several reasons. But it's true that these perpetrators were immediately arrested and convicted to many years in prison as the law dictates. I really have no right to interfere with the judiciary. The truth is that the judiciary responded energetically and that group headed by those two was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you're referring to the Sugic brothers, yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, they may have been arrested on the 26th of August, 1992, which is sometime after these incidents --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Your Honours and Mr. Karadzic, that's in Exhibit D01798, page 11 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But, in fact, they were released before trial, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: You have to ask the courts about that. As far as I know, it's true they were arrested again and tried again. But please don't put me in the awkward position of being a judge, knowing what judgement was made by the courts, et cetera. Our job was to install order. That was the demand of the municipal authorities, and to protect the population regardless of faith of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 05680, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a ruling by the Banja Luka military court on the 15th of February, 1993, releasing Obrenko and Mladen Sugic, because they say that there's no -- there's no need to keep them in custody any longer.

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what that has to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, you just said a moment ago that they were released before they went to trial, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: What I said is this: I learned or heard later that they had been released and re-arrested. But I'm not sure about those details. I can only talk about things that I know for sure. I know for sure that they were convicted to many years in prison. Now, when they were released, whether they were arrested again or not, I really don't know. And there's no need for me to know what the courts did. It was not my job to know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, you're aware, are you not, that the commander of the Celinac Light Infantry Brigade wrote to the military court, seeking their release. And the population of the village of Popovac also sent a document to the military command, asking that they be released. And the and the executive committee of the Celinac Municipal Assembly also wrote a letter asking that their custody be terminated. You're aware of that, aren't you, that the municipal -- the Executive Board wrote to have their custody terminated?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really not aware that they asked for that. I can only suppose that people knocked on all sorts of doors. They didn't come to me, or at least I don't remember. But if they did come to me, they would know my answer and my answer would be that all those who were perpetrators had to answer for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour and Mr. Karadzic, those are Exhibits P3610, 3611, and 3612. Your Honour, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. First of all, the witness hasn't been able to comment on this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just let me ask one question. Mr. Kovacevic, you agree, although you do not know the exact date, that these brothers were once released before they were arrested again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's true, but I'm saying this only from memory, that I heard about it. It doesn't have to be correct. It's probable that they were released, but all I know for sure is that they were arrested and convicted to many years' imprisonment. I mean, it's not valid if I know it just from what somebody told me. If I had read a court decision, then that would be valid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this is the court decision presented to you, so you would argue this is not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not arguing it's not correct or that it's incorrect. I really have nothing to do with this. I don't know why I would have to know. I was just the president of a municipality, not of a court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That brings me to my second objection -- reason for the objection, and that is that you note that the judge or one of the judges who made this decision, Nikola Tomasevic is written on the third line of the English, we asked for a subpoena for Judge Tomasevic so he could explain exactly why this person was released and what pressures, if any, were put to bear on the judiciary and you denied that motion. So we think it would be unfair for the Prosecution to be able to admit this document while at the same time similar or more probative evidence is being excluded from the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, the judge who signed this decision was not Tomasevic, if you could assist --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- in that part?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was signed by the president of the Chamber, but the other two members of the Chamber are listed and Judge Tomasevic was one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see his name, read his name. Would you like to add anything, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, in our submissions, this document impeaches this witness's evidence. We seek to have it admitted. If the Defence want to call this witness, then if we have a document that impeaches his evidence, we -- it should be allowed to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber, by majority, is of the view that this document has nothing to do with the issue of fairness that Mr. Robinson raised. The Chamber, by majority, is of the opinion that we have basis to admit this document through this witness, in the sense that it contradicts with the witness's evidence and as well as the foundational question through which this document could be admitted through this witness. Shall we assign a number for this. I didn't say by majority, with Judge Baird dissenting.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document receives Exhibit Number P6578, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, it's correct, is it not, that -- well, it is correct, it's a fact that Obrenko Sugic was sentenced -- tried and sentenced in 2002 by the Banja Luka District Court to 15 years' imprisonment for his participation in the killings of ten civilians. You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I am aware that he took part in that incident. As for the number of years he was sentenced to later on, I really don't know exactly how many, but it is a well-known thing that he took part in that incident, this unfortunate incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 25802, please. And, I'm sorry, we don't have an English translation at the moment. I have an English translation of a media summary that was done -- not a media summary, a summary that was done by OHR in Banja Luka which I will call up in one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have much more with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have two -- I have three topics that I wish to cover and I would seek to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much longer do you expect you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would hope to be able to do it in 15 minutes. It took a rather long time to get -- to go through the first two documents with the witness, when I was simply wanting a plain reading of the document, it took a lot longer than I had expected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said here a moment ago that Obrenko Sugic was involved in an incident. We can see here that the Banja Luka District Court verdict on the 8th of May, 2002, sentences him to 15 years for murders that were committed on the 7th of July, the 13th of July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber does not see the need on your part to go through with these kind of documents with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 23 of your statement that the Crisis Staff was independent and didn't take any instructions. You know that Branko Djeric had earlier sent instructions for the work of the Serbian municipal Crisis Staffs dated the 26th of April, 1992 - and that's Exhibit P03459 - and the authorities in Celinac received and implemented this decision -- these instructions, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't understand the question. Which document? What is all of this about? What is the point of this question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you can go to page 23 of your statement, you've got it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you is that the authorities in Celinac received Mr. Djeric's instructions dated the 26th of April and they actually implemented their decision -- these instructions when they -- when they set up the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 25780, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see where that is written, that I was sent by Djeric and that I accepted that. I really don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Mr. Kovacevic, that's what I'm putting to you. The document you see on the screen is a document that is signed by you, yes, setting up the Celinac Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what you're saying is something different and what the document says is something different. What I see is a document of the Crisis Staff and there's no denying that, and I am the president of the Crisis Staff, Sveto Kovacevic. And I don't see any Djeric's instructions, non-instructions, I did not notice that, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, but if we were to look at the decision -- Djeric's instructions, which are P3459, we can see that paragraphs in those instructions echo the wording in paragraphs in this decision signed by you?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, you will have to ask Djeric. Djeric, the then-prime minister, that he sent something to me and that that was -- I don't know. At least I don't remember that or it's been deleted from my memory or -- if this is written on the basis of the government, if you think that that is it, well probably -- well, if that's what you think, in paragraph 6 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have the B/C/S actually on the other side of the screen where the current English translation is of P3459.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, we can see there that paragraphs 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 of the Celinac Crisis Staff decision repeats the wording of paragraphs 1, 3, 6, 7, 8, and 14 of the Djeric instructions.

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you think that these are Djeric's instructions --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to the second --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: -- just show me the last page --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- second page --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: -- let me see that, please do refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kovacevic, you were following these instructions when you set up your Celinac Crisis Staff, were you not?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. No --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you -- I mean, can I just say one sentence? Throughout the world and in our part of the world, where there is a crisis, a Crisis Staff is formed. That is based on the Law on Self-Protection and Social Self-Protection. Even if this had not come, it would have been formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this document, 25780.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6579, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 4, page 63, what the witness said was not captured, that this is based on the Law on All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection, meaning ONOSZ. It would be easier if we were to call it that way because actually we've already admitted that law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you said in paragraph 10 of your statement that there were no conditions to form War Presidencies. You know that Mr. Karadzic issued a decision on the 31st of May, 1992, creating War Presidencies. And that's Exhibit P2369. And that this, in fact, was implemented in Celinac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Do refresh my memory. Is there some document so that I could say something?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you can answer my question. The Celinac Crisis Staff was renamed the Celinac War Presidency, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably. I cannot remember now when and how, but I assume that that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, if we go back to the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 65 ter number 25778. This is the session of the 28th of July Municipal Assembly. Page 42 of the B/C/S and page 30 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We can see agenda item 6, verification of decisions and solutions adopted by the Crisis Staff or the Celinac municipality War Presidency. We also see in the document that was issued on the 23rd of July, 1992, War Presidency is the -- in the signature block of the decision on the status of the non-Serb civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think there was no translation, interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do you hear the translation now, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, we see here item 6, this is the minutes of the -- for the 28th of July, 1992, Municipal Assembly meeting, and it talks about verification of decisions and solutions adopted by the Crisis Staff or the Celinac municipality War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Give me -- give me the agenda --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Agenda --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: -- on the screen I --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Agenda item 6 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Next page in English -- in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you see it there, don't you, the reference to War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I never denied that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you were interviewed in Banja Luka by representatives of the OTP on the 26th of February, 2003, you were trying to be helpful and truthful during that interview, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And your memory would have been fresher ten years ago than it is now, yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I just want to confirm something you said in that interview and that was that all the municipality presidents would convene on Mondays for meetings in the municipal building in Banja Luka; correct? And the time-period I'm talking about is May, June, and July 1992. This is what you said when you were interviewed, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. I said that that was the idea, this plan. Now, whether they met, I'm not sure. That there was a plan, yes, but I think that they did not meet. Now, whether they did meet, I really don't know because I was carrying out other duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 25771, please. This is on page 31 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you were asked at line 7: "Did you ever meet the presidents of the other Crisis Staffs?" And you said: "Presidents of other Crisis Staffs? "For example, Rasula from Sanski Most? "Yes, probably, yes, that was normal. "Were there meetings of all the Presidents of Municipalities of the Crisis Staffs of other municipalities ?" And you said: "On Mondays, all the public -- all the Presidents of Municipalities would convene, some people would come, some wouldn't, on Mondays. But we have to differentiate. My ... municipality didn't have the same problems as Sanski Most had ..." So that's what you said. And then further down the page you say that presidents of municipalities -- you were asked --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the relevant page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I don't have that reference just at the moment, Your Honour, I'm sorry. It's the only reference in my whole examination I don't have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you -- it was then put to you, you say the presidents of municipalities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's wait. Let's locate the page. It's impossible at all? Take a look at this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, perfect. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you see there, Mr. Kovacevic, you stated that: "On Mondays, all the public -- all the Presidents of Municipalities would convene, some ... would come, some wouldn't ..." You see that there?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I see that, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then down the bottom of the page you're asked: "You say the Presidents of Municipalities would -- of the Crisis Staffs would meet on Mondays? "Yes. "And where would those meetings take place? "At the municipality." And you're asked: "Which municipality?" And then you say: "Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I suggest that we ask the witness to read out something from the previous page so that we see how these interpreters are going to interpret this. The translation here is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I'm not dealing with the previous page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, that -- probably he was referring to the page you read out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But witness must have heard Ms. Sutherland's question. So let us see whether he can answer the question. What is your question, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That this is what you said, that the presidents of the municipalities -- the presidents of the Crisis Staffs were meeting weekly in Banja Luka. That's right, isn't it, that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I'm not denying that I said or that I did not say. But if there was a meeting and if we did meet, that was the reason -- that was actually a conversation, an exchange of views. Now, whether there was something missing, whether we could help each other, whether there's some new information in terms of the economy, logistics, and other troubles that befell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think there's a need for me to tender this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Two pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But perhaps we should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would ask that it be MFI'd subject to the verification of the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If there's an issue, I would like the accused to file it in writing. We do not do this, following our practice, where there's a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, we'll make a request to the translation section to look at this document again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. First I would like the Defence to check the transcript -- the translation first and raise it afterwards. We are not sure whether there is a problem or not. We'll assign a number for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6580, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But do we need to call the witness again, then, if he's supposed to confirm what it was that he was asked and what he answered and whether he asked -- whether he answered a question that had been asked on the basis of a wrong translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, let's see whether it's necessary, then we'll do so. But I take it you have time to review whether there's a translation issue and raise it during his -- your re-examination if necessary. You're done, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have this last topic that I wish to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for 45 minutes. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you're indicating in paragraphs 6, 7, 9, 12, 15, and 37 that you're a member of the Main Board, SDS Main Board. And as such, you're familiar with the workings of the SDS and the positions taken and decisions issued by the Main Board and the party. I want to examine what you told the OTP in 2003 when you were interviewed about your role in and knowledge of the SDS Main Board, and I want to take you as quickly as possible through five excerpts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can go, please, to B/C/S pages 8 and 9 but starting on page 8, and the English page 10. That is 65 ter number 25771, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacevic, you were asked here of the meetings -- talking about the Main Board meetings that you did attend, do you remember the topics that were discussed, the SDS Main Board meetings? And you say: "I don't really know. I don't remember anything specific. I don't remember anything. The SDS didn't have its own formations, so I don't remember anything specific that I could stress right now ..." And it's correct, isn't it, that you couldn't remember any topic that was discussed at Main Board meetings; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. It is just the opposite. I said then that I didn't remember all of the details, but that I agreed with the programme and the statute. I suppose I said that. I don't know whether that was recorded or not, but that was true then and it is still true now. And I apologise, I need to finish the thought. People were afraid, there was a feeling of terror. I was also afraid. And later on when I read everything, when I examined the situation, when I realised that some documents were missing, you have to appreciate the kind of situation that reigned at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you talking about in 2003, when you were interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. In 2003 I did not have any documents. I had not been prepared and my memory had not been jogged. I joined the different company and economic entity to work there. You can ask me anything. I'm not avoiding anything. Now that my memory has been jogged, I can tell you everything. At that time I didn't have the necessary documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you were asked a simple question about what topics were discussed at Main Board meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could move to transcript page 11, B/C/S pages 9 and 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you're asked here, starting in the English it's at line 6: "Now, there must have been a reason for the SDS as a party having a Main Board. What was the reason?" And you said: "Every party has a Main Board." And you were asked: "Right. And what is a function of a Main Board in a party?" And you said: "You need to look at the Statute and read it to see what the activities of the party are and what the activities of the Main Board would be." So you weren't even able to state what the functions of a Main Board were within the party; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, if you looked at the matter more attentively, you could have seen that every party had a Main Board and that if you wanted to know something you should refer to the Statute. I can now explain why I said that and I repeat that every party has a Main Board and it is the most important body in every party, including the Serbian Democratic Party. What I said then was for you to look at the Statute, but there is nothing odd about that and there is no reason for me to state anything differently to what I stated at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender the two pages that I've just taken the witness to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that your last question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour -- not my last question, but apparently it's the practice to tender the pages as we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you have more questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much more?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have three more excerpts that I wish to take the witness to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll add those two pages, Ms. Sutherland, but please conclude your cross-examination in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can go to B/C/S page 6 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. This is the interview we -- part of which we admitted already or is it a different interview?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So P6576 -- no, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 6580, I think if my memory serves me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add those pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 7 of your statement you discuss the plenum held on the 16th of February, 1993, at Jahorina, as if you attended the meeting, but you didn't, did you?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: What made you conclude that I wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, if we go to your OTP interview, 2003, page 6 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S, you say: "I was a member of the Main Board for a while." And you were asked: "For what period were you a member of the Main Board?" You say: "Let's say from 1991 and when I moved to Metal company, I didn't go anywhere." Now, it's right that you moved to the Metal company in Banja Luka in June 1992, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if I --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: But I didn't stop being a member of the Main Board. I said that it is possible that I attended fewer meetings, but I did attend them and I remained a member of the Main Board until 1995 or 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, if I can take you to B/C/S page 6 again, so on that same page, and the English transcript page 7, you're asked: "Did you attend any meetings of the SDS Main Board?" You said: "I was, I would, I went occasionally and when I moved to the Metal company, I stopped going all together and I didn't -- I would go rarely actually, only if something was going on in Banja Luka." And then a couple of questions later you say: "I stopped going because I had other obligations, other duties, so yes, afterwards rarely, almost never." And I can take you to one more excerpt, which is English page 11 and B/C/S page 10, you say -- you were asked: "How long were you a member of this party, Mr. Kovacevic?" You say: "As I told you already, I was a member of a Municipal Board and I only went a few times because I was president of the municipality. After that I was also a member of, also a member of the Main Board, but once I moved to the Metal company, I don't think I went a single time." So you're saying that you stopped going all together basically and only attended if the meeting was in Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. You have two different kinds of impression. First of all you said that I didn't attend meetings after joining the metal company and then you said at first I did attend and later I didn't. It is true that later I didn't. What does it mean "later"? In 1994, 1995, or perhaps even earlier than that because I had other commitments. However, at first and when you implied that "later" means 2002 and 2003, that's not correct. But if you implied that "later" is later, then it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender these pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you're trying to tell this Court through your statement and testimony that you're familiar with the SDS. You tell the OTP --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- that you never attended meetings and you don't know how the SDS Main Board functions. So you say one thing to one entity, i.e., Mr. Karadzic, for use in this court, and you tell another one to the OTP, completely contradictory?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not correct. May I be allowed to explain? You are trying to permutate my statements. It is true that I was a member of the Main Board, and at the moment when I provided a statement my memory had not been jogged. But if you're implying that during the later part of my office I attended fewer meetings, that's correct. However, if you're saying that at first I didn't, then we're talking about a totally different thing. It is true what I said then when my memory had not been jogged; however, once my memory was jogged, then I realised that what I was saying was true and that's why I continue claiming the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellencies. I'll try to reduce the number of those questions to a minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacevic, could you please tell us this: When it comes to the Main Board, while the work of the party was frozen between the month of March until February 1993, did the Main Board meet at least once?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: During that period when the work of the party was frozen, the Main Board was never convened to meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was suggested to you that you don't know what the function of the Main Board are, and we can see here that you are referring the Prosecutor to the Statute. Is it true that you didn't know what the functions of the Main Board were?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I phrased my answer properly or not, but I know what the functions of the Main Board were, what its tasks were. I know it very well. I know what the Main Board was, how decisions were made in a democratic way. Obviously my memory was eventually refreshed. For a number of years I was part of the corporate world. I had never been involved in politics before then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber which body adopts the party platform or programme and when does that happen?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It happens at the Assembly meeting, and the Main Board is the body that implements the Assembly's decision. The Main Board runs the party between two Assembly meetings. The president of the party only co-ordinates the work of the party, as I have already stated. It is the Main Board that makes the decisions and so on and so forth and so on and so forth, but this is all in the Statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can the Main Board discuss the party programme at every meeting and can it alter it before the Assembly session? Who is allowed to change the programme of the party or the platform of the party?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Only the Assembly can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, did you participate in the work of the Assembly sessions that issued the programme?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I did. I was also elected by the Assembly, and from the very first moment I agreed with the programme of the Serbian Democratic Party, which is why I accepted to take part in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When were you appointed the CO of Metal?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When you look at the documents, you will see that it was on the 1st of June, 1992; however, I was still in charge of the municipality because new president had not been elected. That's how things are according to our statute, but if -- so if you look at the documents, it would be on the 1st of June, but I was still in the position of the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How often did the sessions of the Municipal Assembly take place?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I assume -- not only do I assume, I know that it was once a month or twice in exceptional situations. I believe that it was once a month. I'm not sure. I would say that those sessions or those meetings took place once a month throughout that period of four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While the War Presidency existed, how often did that body meet?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It met more often because its work implied taking certain actions, to deal with certain everyday problems. And for that reason its meetings took place more often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you attend every meeting of the War Presidency once you moved to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Before I handed over my duties, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were also asked about the document describing the special status of the 34 people. Can you tell us, out of 1800 why only 34? What drew everybody's attention to them?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: If the Trial Chamber wants to understand me, I would like to say that those 34 men had been previously known to the police. We didn't want to take any action against them for misdemeanours to which they may have reacted. We decided instead to place them under control. Believe me - and I am sure that the Trial Chamber understands - that that decision was very good, that its main purpose was to protect everybody, and that every Muslim to the last is ready to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at P2638. I believe that's the number of the document that I would like to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who did the threat come from? You mentioned burials, the passage of the troops, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was our estimate, based on the information from various services, that it was not from the authorities but from renegade soldiers or people returning from the front lines of various people who were prone to causing incidents. I don't know how to call these people before this Trial Chamber. But in any case, the threat didn't come from the authorities, either republic or municipal authorities, but from those vagabonds that we were all afraid from, and we were afraid that they might provoke an incident and that as a result of that somebody might get killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the person under number 18 is?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Salih Nezirovic, father's name Kasim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that somebody threw -- an explosion happened in Cafe Charlie [phoen] whose owner was Salih Nezirovic, son of Kasim. Was it justified for that person to be monitored or protected because he was threatened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, just a second. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I don't know what document Mr. Karadzic is referring to when he's talking about the explosion in the cafe. Could he inform us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. This was a piece of news aired on Radio Banja Luka. At least two names are mentioned, Ismet Behonjic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Beharic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ismet Beharic, somebody threw a grenade on his house and at Charlie cafe whose owner was Salih Nezirovic, where a grenade was also thrown resulting in an explosion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, I told you about the various newspapers and various pieces of news that were not correct. About me, they said that I hid my son so he wouldn't join the army and he was 9 or 10 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many times and on what occasions was a curfew imposed?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, curfew was imposed only in times of unrest. And when one group of Serb fighters got killed on the Vlasic front line, we were afraid of incidents in town so we imposed a curfew to protect the entire population, the Serbs and Muslims alike, to prevent a robbery and murders and such, for everyone, the Serbs, the Muslims, and the few Croats that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who was subject to the curfew when these men were killed?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The entire population was subject to the curfew. Even policemen and fighting men, the entire population of the municipality, regardless of whether they were Muslim, Serb, or Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, paragraph 30 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me ask you just simply, Mr. Witness, Mr. Kovacevic, if your protection was to protect these individuals, you could simply have said that these individuals are protected and it is prohibited that the public attack these individuals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how to explain this to you. Of course some people were afraid. My next-door neighbour was a Muslim, the headmaster of the school. Of course I communicated with them. Of course we made arrangements and had understandings with each other. I respected his opinion a great deal. He didn't move out throughout the war. Of course we talked to the people among the Muslims who had the greatest authority, and we were trying to deal with things to see how to resolve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now look at 25771, Serbian page 31, which was not translated well. I'll give you the English page in a second. I cannot find the corresponding page in English. Sorry, the English page is 31 and the Serbian page is 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please read beginning with line 22 through line 28 so that it can be interpreted properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I would like the interpreters to interpret from -- directly from Mr. Kovacevic's testimony, not from the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let them ignore the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, aloud, and slowly.

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: "You see, we from -- we -- all the presidents of municipalities were called on Mondays. Some came, some didn't, on Mondays. But we have to distinguish, my municipality did not have the same problems like, for instance, Sanski Most. My municipality to maintain peace and then" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, do not insert new sentences. Just read the passage as it is.

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: "My municipality to maintain peace. And over there, there are other problems. I have no inter-ethnic problems. My neighbours, can I just say this? My neighbours have been in the war" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just read out the passage you were asked. We can't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: He did read, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He omitted then --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, he read: "Can I just say this?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, start over, without inserting any new sentences, slowly, beginning with line 22.

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: "You see, we from -- we all presidents of municipalities were called on Mondays. Some came, some didn't, on Mondays. But we have to distinguish. My municipality did not have the same problems like, for instance, Sanski Most. My municipality to maintain peace, and over there there are other problems. I have no inter-ethnic problems. "My neighbours, can I just say this? My neighbours have been in the war. I'll enumerate them. And stayed throughout the war. Some people, individuals, would come and ask: What is this? We have to go. They had great trust in me."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's now interpreted properly if I followed well. So you said you had no inter-ethnic problems in your municipality and that the Muslims came to you asking: What's going on? Do we have to go? And what would you tell them?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I would tell them that the Serb authorities of Republika Srpska and I as a part of these authorities on the municipal level will do everything to prevent any excesses, forced migration, moving out of people, transfer, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In one paragraph of your statement you mention that some Muslims came to you and made some statements. When was that and why did they come to you?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: You see, my next-door neighbour was Irfan Tataric. In the last few months, he was organising a wedding for his son Muamer. He called me to ask where to send the invitation. I said: I'm here in Celinac. I'll come by and pick up my invitation. I took the invitation. I sat down with him and had coffee with him. The entire discussion was precisely about the same things that we are discussing today. We talked about the forcible eviction of people that some terrorists had tried to effect; and he said: Thank you, Mr. Kovacevic. We know that the Serb authorities of Republika Srpska had done everything to protect us and you in your position. I later attended the wedding and he thanked me and he made that statement that I brought here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say you -- he offered a statement?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: He offered me that statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show 1D09544.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I object to the use of this statement with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Statement? What he's going to upload is a statement of others?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, before uploading this document, why could you not ask the witness your question first?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I asked, Your Excellency, on what occasion -- for what reason that Muslim offered him a statement, and I referred to one statement on which the witness gave evidence orally, evidence that was disputed by the Prosecution. I am not offering the statement. I'm just trying to show how the authorities treated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the document you are going to show the witness was the statement this witness allegedly received from the individual he referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's a statement that is signed and speaks to matters that the Prosecution disputed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who shall I hear from first? Can I hear from you first, Ms. Sutherland, on the point of objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are third party -- this one in particular he -- is a third-party statement prepared for the purposes, I would say, of these current proceedings. And under the Trial Chamber's practice, these sorts of statements don't come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the admissibility issue. So what's the point of objecting to putting to the -- to the putting of this document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has asked -- has been asked the question about what the witness discussed with him. He's answered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So there is no need to refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that your point?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, the statement shouldn't be allowed to be used to bolster this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Bolstering, he confirmed already.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But it's a third-party statement of another witness that we can't cross-examine. Your ruling is that third-party statements not prepared for the purposes of a current criminal proceeding can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we do not admit them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But this is a -- this is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not -- the accused didn't say that he was tendering that document. He was going to put that document to the witness, so asking questions about the statement, alleged statement. I thought your objection was --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- something like that in the circumstances the witness confirmed everything, there is no need to refresh his memory, but you are saying that if something is not admissible it's prohibited from showing the document to the witness itself?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, I'm saying that he's asked the witness the questions about what the witness -- the third-party person is purported to have said. The witness has answered that. He shouldn't be allowed to use this third-party statement with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you assist us, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we discussed this, myself and Dr. Karadzic, and I told him that my understanding of the Chamber's practice was that third-party statements are admissible if they are -- but not those that are prepared for -- as for testimony because Rule 92 bis would probably be lex specialis to that. And so he said that he would, instead of trying to get the document -- have the document admitted, simply elicit oral testimony from the witness about this -- the fact that what he has been saying in court through his cross-examination is supported by other information that he would like to bring to the attention of the Court. So that's what Dr. Karadzic is trying to do, and it's up to you whether you think that that violates the spirit of your decision that would not admit the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it that's the statement of Tataric, Irfan Tataric; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies, yes. And there's also one statement from Ismet Topic, but I'll deal with them in just one -- with one or two sentences to see if it's -- if it's consistent with the witness's experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So he talked about -- the witness himself talked about the event regarding Irfan Tataric at length from transcript page 83 to 84, and he confirmed that he offered the statement to the witness himself. I don't see the need for you to put that document when it is apparent that the Chamber is not going to admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then I'll ask the question this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there some Toplic houses attacked and one Fikret Toplic was killed?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that one man Fikret Toplic was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll read to you now what Ismet Toplic told you, that this was done by a group --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Again, now Mr. Karadzic is going to another exhibit -- another document that he put on his Rule 92 ter notification to be used as an additional exhibit, and it's the same thing, it's a third-party statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you put your question first without referring to document or evidence or statement? If you are putting something that is written in other document, that's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether this Fikret Toplic is related to Ismet Toplic; and what did Ismet Toplic say to you or write about this incident?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Of course they are related. I don't know exactly how or how closely. All the Toplic family lives in one street. But almost all the Muslims, including the Toplic family, still come up to me regularly to this day, thanking me for the fact that the authorities had protected the Muslims and they did not fare like some others did. And especially this Toplic is a person I meet very often because he is a carpenter, I think, and I see him rather often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what did Bajro Jusic say about who was responsible, and what was the attitude of the authorities and your personal attitude to these incidents?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was a group of hooligans, homeless hooligans who were responsible. They wanted to tarnish the entire municipality with its authorities and all the Serbian people. Everybody knows that. This Jusic, this Bajro Jusic has his own car repair shop where he works there with his son, and when I take my car there we often reminisce and remember these events. And he is among many others who thank me for the fact that the republic authorities and the municipal authorities suppressed these incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that I intervened in the case of the Bastezi village.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show D102, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this document before you? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. A lot of such documents came to the MUP, not only to the MUP but to other offices too. Of course I meant this document and there were many other similar ones. I know that you constantly wrote and warned that we must protect the population, prevent looting, and it was discussed at the Main Board. And all the people at the head of municipalities implemented this and there were much fewer incidents in those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is dated 19 August. You said that the prosecution authorities conducted an on-site investigation immediately?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. The man was prosecuted and tried.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show D1798.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did this happen, do you remember, this killing?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date, but it was at the time of those unfortunate incidents in the municipality. It was either before or after, but it is that period, the summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These names from this -- from this folder, do you know these names? Do they ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Sugic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Against --

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand, President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The injured party. Who's that?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The injured party is the Muslims and the perpetrator is a Serb. We talked about them a moment ago. Of course they were sentenced to many years in prison. For how long -- I mean, really. I see that the centre of public security has all that information and, indeed, that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please say what the name of the investigating judge is? And who is this person, number 3, ethnicity, this doctor, or rather, this pathologist? Actually, who was the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Jefto Jankovic. It so happens that I know him personally, he's a Serb. And number 3 is Nijaz Julum, he's a Muslim from -- well, I think he's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, please, the first three numbers, the on-site investigation is attended by?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Vesna Mijovic [phoen], Oljaca --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Srdjan?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Srdjan. Granulic Nijaz?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Crnalic Halid?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Halid Crnalic. Yes, the letters are small, President, so -- yeah, cannot see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This pathologist, Halid, what is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: He's an expert of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This exhibit has 44 pages and this is the only thing that I wanted to deal with -- well, yes, all right. This is the 13th of August; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: 13th of August, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kovacevic, thank you for having come to testify. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: SVETO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you too, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Kovacevic. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are free to go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While -- before we hear the evidence of the next witness, I'd like to deal with this matter now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's about the Defence filing of today, precautionary Rule 94 bis notice, Marko Sladojevic. The Chamber is simply puzzled by this filing. So could you tell us what the Defence is seeking through this submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're seeking to avoid any objection at the time of Mr. Sladojevic's testimony on the basis of he's offering expert testimony and that Rule 94 bis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you refer to his evidence as expert testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we don't believe it is expert testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Aha, yes. I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's why it's called precautionary notice. We did this once before with the testimony of Steven Joudry who was a ballistics person talking about one incident in Sarajevo, but also gave information beyond that of the facts that he observed. And we were concerned that perhaps if Mr. Sladojevic's evidence is objected to on the grounds that it's more properly considered expert evidence, then we wanted to make sure that we had covered the base of having filed such a notice. That's the purpose of doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow. What about the dead-line for 94 bis application at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, well, that applied to our first set of witnesses, was the 27th of August. But Mr. Sladojevic was not contemplated to be called as a witness until the new set of witnesses for Count 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 27 August 2012.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Right. So Mr. Sladojevic was not on that list. However, when you gave us the 25 additional hours, then we submitted a new list pursuant to your instructions and Mr. Sladojevic was on the new list. And therefore, that's when his expert notice came up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you agree that he is not an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's our position, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then what is he going to testify as a fact witness or as a -- yes, what's the content of his testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's going to testify to the compilation of statements made by Dr. Karadzic on different topics at different times during the course of the time-period covered by the indictment. You'll see in the notice that we analogised his testimony to that of Jean-Rene Ruez or Dean Manning who amalgamated essentially bits and pieces of information that had been admitted or not admitted during the trial and presented the Chamber with a coherent picture of those events and that's what Mr. Sladojevic has proposed to do for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
