utterances.text: I don't think it's appropriate to compare him to Dean Manning or Jean-Rene Ruez. But separate from that, why do we need to rely on Mr. Sladojevic to have compilation of Mr. Karadzic's speech or et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, because this presents the speeches to the Chamber in a way in which they could be more readily understood in their context by both topic and chronologically. So you have bits and pieces of his utterances in all kinds of forms, intercepted conversations, Assembly sessions, documents admitted from the bar table, documents admitted through witnesses, but it's a central part of our case, especially with respect to Count 1, as to what Dr. Karadzic's mens rea was and this is collecting in a coherent way for the Chamber all of those things and presenting it so -- in a way that you could understand it and apply it when you have to decide Count 1 and the other counts as to his mens rea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why not bar table motion, Mr. Robinson, for those which are not in evidence? This study is nothing -- nothing more than a bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, getting the documents admitted into evidence is another matter, but we think that the utility of the testimony and his report is the way in which the materials are collected so that you could see, for example, what did Dr. Karadzic say about allegations that there was unlawful shellings in Sarajevo. And these are all over the record. We have 9.000 exhibits in the case, but Mr. Sladojevic puts in maybe 2 or 3 pages what Dr. Karadzic said on that topic. It seems to me that's useful for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So he's going to make closing argument on behalf of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No much more so than Mr. Ruez or Mr. Manning made their closing arguments on behalf of the Prosecutor by compiling information that was largely already in evidence, but in a way which made it understandable to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to make any observation, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the Court seems well seized of this matter. First of all, with or without the precautionary notice, we would never have mistaken Mr. Sladojevic for an expert on this subject. Number two, then I guess the next step is for me to call myself in rebuttal as a witness in response to Mr. Sladojevic's submissions as a purported witness. It's very clear, as the Court noted, that this is in the guise of -- this is something painted as witness -- appropriate witness testimony, which is obviously provided for in the form of a final brief or closing submissions. That's precisely the purpose those mechanisms of the trial process are to serve, and we should move forward toward those as expeditiously as possible without the intervention of invented witness categories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Only, Mr. President, that I have still yet to hear any distinction between what the Prosecution itself did in their case and -- with Manning, with Jean-Rene Ruez, even Dorothea Hanson who compiled all the Crisis Staff documents and put it into one document or Christian Nielsen who compiled all of these other documents. So the Prosecution was the one who presented a so-called closing argument through their witnesses by compiling dispersed materials and having a witness summarise them. So we would like to, at least with one witness, do the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before hearing from the Prosecution, those were recognised in their quality as expert witnesses, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not Mr. Ruez or Mr. Manning, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I'm talking about Dorothea Hanson and Christian Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, although their expertise came through their experience working for the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Sladojevic has now been four, almost five years working for Dr. Karadzic's Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I would -- I was going to say, Mr. President, that that submission, with respect, is both simultaneously disingenuous and rude. First of all, the Court itself already made the distinction and indicated to Mr. Robinson that that was a specious decision. Notwithstanding that, Mr. Robinson says to the Court: Well, I haven't heard enough from you even though you've just expressed your position on the subject. As the Court has made clear, the expertise of Ms. Hanson, Mr. Nielsen, and the other Prosecution witnesses was tested, was announced, tested in full and over a long period of time. The backdrop to the efforts of Mr. Ruez and Mr. Manning are well-known to the Court and are markedly and visibly distinct from that of Mr. Sladojevic. The -- I mean, we can begin with the fact that Mr. Sladojevic's role in this proceeding, as I understand it, is in the matter of an advocate. So the first question he'd have to -- I mean, he is not even in a position to offer opinions about Mr. Karadzic contrary to the obligations he assumes as the advocate. So he is, by virtue of his very position, precluded from the very role that Mr. Robinson wants him to assume. These are such markedly distinct categories that it's almost difficult to discuss it, but I return to my initial observation which is that the Court dismissed that purported distinction at the outset and yet Mr. Robinson pretended not to hear and simply overrode the Court's determination made at the very outset of this discussion. That's not appropriate. It's, I might add, a reflection of a kind of persistence that we've seen before that keeps matters before the Court when they really have been disposed of. This matter should be disposed of quickly because it is completely unfounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will give a ruling in due course, probably tomorrow. But before we go on, at the end of that filing you stated that Mr. Sladojevic is expected to testify at the end of February or beginning of March. Did you mean to say Mr. Sladojevic is the last witness for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before Dr. Karadzic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we -- the Chamber has informed of its calculation that Defence case may close at the end of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's one of the reasons why we've put "end of February" in that filing, but our own calculations - which may be unduly optimistic in terms of the efficiency of Dr. Karadzic in conducting his examination-in-chief and re-examination - but our own calculations still holding out some hope that there will be some witnesses in March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said -- just Mr. Karadzic is going conduct his examination-in-chief and re-examination. Could you be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm meaning that in between now and the end of our case, we are urging Dr. Karadzic to be as brief as possible with these witnesses so that we can conserve as much time and we can have as many witnesses as possible. And if he does that, our calculations are that we might be into March before we reach the testimony of Mr. Sladojevic and Dr. Karadzic, who would be the last two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wondered whether you were referring to the mode of examination-in-chief with respect to Mr. Karadzic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, that is going to be -- was going to be the subject of a filing we were going to make later in the week, but the mode of examination-in-chief of Dr. Karadzic's testimony would be the narrative mode as far as we're proposing. I might indicate, we had originally planned on 32 hours of examination for Dr. Karadzic, which we were going to ask the Chamber for permission for me to ask him questions. And as the case progressed and we saw that the number of hours we had didn't seem to be adequate, we looked for ways in which we could reduce that and decided that we could cut it in half by having him testify in the narrative form. And so we were going to ask the Chamber or propose that he testify in the narrative form, and therefore we have now allocated 16 hours to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll leave it at that. Shall we bring in the next witness. We'll start Mr. Stakic's evidence, but tomorrow we'll begin with Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that is the arrangement we've made. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours, and all those who are present. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stakic. Please be seated. And make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the counsel assisting Mr. Stakic introduce himself for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. My name is John Ostojic. I'm here on behalf of Mr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Stakic, although I take it you know this very well, but before you commence your evidence I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the international Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer incriminates you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that would amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that might indicate that you have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC
utterances.text: Good day, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, let us pause, both you and I, and let us speak slowly so that everything would be recorded in the transcript. Did you give my Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court 1D9501.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the screen before you, do you see the first page of that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I read it and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the last page so that Dr. Stakic could identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully convey what you stated to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, the same as those that were put to you by my team, would your answers basically be the same as those contained in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC
utterances.text: Just one small remark in relation to 24 and 32, those two paragraphs. My lawyer drew my attention to that. I agree with what is written in the Serbian language; however, my lawyer, who speaks English, drew my attention to two things in these two paragraphs. In his view, the translation not very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could paragraph 24 please be displayed both in English and in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you help us, Dr. Stakic, this paragraph, 24 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, we haven't got it in English. Could we have paragraph 24 in English? Yes, now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please help us with this. What is correct in Serbian and incorrect in English?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC
utterances.text: The third sentence in the third line: "Simo Drljaca did that and that is the only thing I know with regard to Omarska." And in English it says only "intelligence." My lawyer told me that that would better be translated by using a different word because this is my information. It's not that I had some kind of service through which I got some kind of special information. Do you see what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So "my knowledge" or "my information" would be better?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think that -- well, could the professional interpreters here please say what they've got to say because I don't really understand English. It is quite possible that it's that word, but I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] I know -- [Interpretation] I know, that's what they said. [In English] "Simo Drljaca did that and that is the only thing I know with regard to Omarska ..." [Interpretation] Are you satisfied with that now, the only thing that you knew?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that I had information about. Also, the same thing is repeated two sentences further down. This resounded in Prijedor and then my sentence says: "According to what I know or according to my knowledge ..." and again the word "intelligence" is used here, "according to my intelligence ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, could this please be taken into account, could it be corrected. So what else did you say, paragraph 32?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC
utterances.text: 32, yes, very briefly. In the first sentence. I'm sorry. Could you please have both the English version and this version of paragraph 32 here. "I first met Dr. Karadzic in mid-1991 when we had certain problems in our party in Prijedor ..." Whereas here it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Our station."

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC
utterances.text: "Station," yes, that's what my lawyer told me and my lawyer said that this is not a good translation. Again, I would like to ask the interpreters here to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it would be in "our party"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC
utterances.text: In our political party, the local one in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing all of that in mind, is the statement correct now and will your answers to my questions, the same questions, be the same as those contained in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, provided that these corrections are made. I repeat, they would be the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I would like to tender this statement according to Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And about the associated exhibits, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're offering ten associated exhibits. One of them on our list has already been admitted and that is number 14663, which is P3535.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note 65 ter 17930, referenced at paragraph 20, that is also in evidence. It's the first few pages of Exhibit P3536. And with regard to 1D09763, referenced at paragraph 28, this is a 405-page document and as of the first thing this morning there was no translation uploaded. In the last few hours we've had a partial translation uploaded. There are 12 English pages now which appear to correspond to pages 1 through 9 and page 399 of this exhibit. So we now have translated a total of ten pages of this 400-plus-page document and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I thought it was translation of the format, but it is not the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, the -- it's a complete translation of the contents of the document, but only ten pages of it. So the translation is incomplete, whereas the -- but the witness's comments on the document, it's clear he was shown the entire document, his comments appear to relate to the entire document. So in our submission, if Dr. Karadzic wishes to rely on this he should lead it live and it should be MFI'd in accordance with the normal procedure. Thank you. And apart from that, no other objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, with respect to that document 1D9763, unfortunately we had some problems. The first one was that the translation section refused to translate the entire document, and so we don't have any objections to your MFI-ing it and directing them to translate the rest of it. The other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, we have already admitted part of it as MFI P6501. I'm not sure why it is P exhibit. First -- I think first page and page 62 have been admitted, marked for identification. But why do we need entire document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, as you can see from the statement, the point is to show that there were Muslims being treated throughout the period in the hospital. So the document can speak to that, but if you would like us to select other pages from that document we can do that. But it doesn't seem like there's any harm to having the entire document admitted since his evidence refers to the document as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And with respect to 1D9765 and 6 referred to in para 28, I'd like to draw the attention of the parties to para -- the languages used in para 28, the last sentence. I would like to note that the fact they were relieved of duties does not mean that their employment was terminated. Besides, these two documents show that those two persons were dismissed from duty in August 1992. So I'm not clear whether this witness is qualifying the meaning of these documents in his statement, so I'd like the accused to lead live with this -- with respect to these documents -- two documents. And so otherwise, we'll admit all the exhibits -- associated exhibits, and in particular with respect to 1D9763, we'll mark it -- we'll -- shall we add it to the Prosecution exhibit or shall we admit it as a separate exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think probably as a separate exhibit. My recollection from the previous use that it was just a reference to one particular page for a particular person. And so this -- since it's the -- the whole document is now going in for a different purpose, I think -- through a Defence witness, it should be given a new number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll mark it for identification as a separate Defence exhibit. The exhibit numbers will be assigned in due course by the Registrar. Apologies for the parties, but the Chamber should rise immediately. So, Mr. Stakic, we'll continue tomorrow sometime in the morning after we will have finished Mr. Beara's evidence. I take it that has been conveyed to the witness and his counsel? Yes, Mr. Ostojic will stay on --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of December, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.
